body:
Why the public sector became important

At independence, India had limited domestic capacity to manufacture heavy machinery, industrial equipment, steel and other basic industrial goods. Private capital and technical resources were insufficient to establish all the large industries required for rapid industrialisation. Many of these industries also required heavy initial investment and had long periods before generating returns.

The government therefore expanded the public sector, in which industrial enterprises are owned or controlled by the government. Public-sector enterprises were expected to establish basic industries, develop infrastructure, provide essential inputs to other industries, reduce dependence on imports and encourage industrial development in less-developed regions.

This approach is often described as developing the commanding heights of the economy under public-sector leadership. It did not mean that private industry was abolished. Public and private enterprises were expected to operate together.

Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956

Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948

The first Industrial Policy Resolution was announced on 6 April 1948. It recognised the importance of both public and private enterprise while giving the State a progressively active role in industrial development.

Arms and ammunition, atomic energy and railway transport were placed under the exclusive responsibility of the Central Government. The State also assumed responsibility for establishing new units in specified basic industries, while the remaining industrial field was open to regulated private enterprise.

Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956

The Industrial Policy Resolution of 30 April 1956 strengthened the public sector's role. It aimed to establish a socialist pattern of society through rapid industrialisation, expansion of heavy industries, prevention of excessive concentration of economic power and reduction of regional inequalities.

The resolution divided industries into 3 categories according to the intended role of the State and private enterprise.

CategoryNumber and State roleExamples
Schedule A17 industries; future development was the exclusive responsibility of the State.Arms and ammunition, atomic energy, iron and steel, coal, mineral oils, heavy electrical machinery and railways.
Schedule B12 industries; the State would progressively expand its role, but private enterprise was not excluded.Fertilizers, machine tools, aluminium, essential drugs and certain transport industries.
Third categoryAll remaining industries; private enterprise generally took the initiative, subject to government regulation.Various consumer goods and other industrial activities.

The categories did not create a completely separate public-private division. Existing private enterprises could continue operating, and the government could participate in industries outside the first category when required by national planning.

Common examination trap

The original Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 formally listed Schedule A and Schedule B. The remaining industries were described as the third category. Many summaries call this Schedule C, but the original resolution did not provide a separate enumerated Schedule C list.

Industrial licensing and import substitution

Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951

The Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 provided a legal framework for government regulation of scheduled industries.

Under Section 11, a new industrial undertaking in a scheduled industry generally required a licence from the Central Government. Section 13 also regulated substantial expansion and certain changes in the location of existing industrial undertakings. The licensing system allowed the government to influence the type, capacity and location of industrial investment.

Industrial licences could be used to encourage investment in backward regions. Industrial units established in economically backward areas could receive concessions such as tax benefits and lower electricity tariffs. The objective was to avoid excessive concentration of industry in already-developed regions.

Import substitution

Import substitution means producing domestically goods that were previously imported. India used tariffs, import restrictions and industrial regulation to protect domestic industries and encourage the production of machinery, steel, chemicals and consumer goods within the country.

This approach helped build an industrial base and reduced dependence on imported manufactured products. However, prolonged protection and excessive licensing could also reduce competition, delay industrial expansion and weaken incentives to improve efficiency.

Development of public-sector heavy industries

The Second Five-Year Plan gave high priority to iron and steel production. Three major integrated public-sector steel plants were established with foreign collaboration.

Steel plantPresent locationCollaborating country
BhilaiChhattisgarhSoviet Union
RourkelaOdishaWest Germany
DurgapurWest BengalUnited Kingdom

Bhilai was then located in Madhya Pradesh; it is now in Chhattisgarh. Rourkela was then in Orissa, now Odisha. Durgapur was established in West Bengal. These plants formed an important part of India's public-sector industrialisation during the Second Plan.

Hindustan Steel Limited was established in 1954 to manage public-sector steel development. The Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) was incorporated in 1973 and subsequently became the major holding company responsible for several integrated steel plants.

Regional imbalance in industrial development

Regional imbalance

Regional imbalance refers to unequal levels of economic development, industrialisation, infrastructure and employment opportunities among different geographical regions.

Industrial development tends to concentrate in locations that already possess favourable conditions. Important factors include:

  • Availability of raw materials such as iron ore, coal and minerals.
  • Reliable electricity, water and transport facilities.
  • Access to ports, railways and major markets.
  • Availability of skilled workers, technical institutions and finance.
  • Existing industrial infrastructure and supporting industries.

Once an industrial centre develops, it attracts additional industries, workers, investment and services. This can create a cycle in which already-developed regions attract more investment while backward regions continue to lag.

The 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution explicitly recognised this problem. It proposed extending infrastructure and industrial opportunities to areas that had remained industrially backward. Public-sector plants, infrastructure investment, industrial licensing and support for small-scale industries were among the instruments used to encourage balanced development.

However, industrial concentration did not disappear. Some regions continued to possess much stronger industrial infrastructure, capital availability and market access than others.

Gujarat's industrial region

Gujarat provides an important example of regional industrial concentration. The Gujarat Industrial Region has its nucleus between Ahmedabad and Vadodara. Other important industrial centres include Bharuch, Koyali, Anand, Rajkot, Surat, Valsad and Jamnagar.

The region developed through a combination of cotton textiles, chemicals, petrochemicals, engineering, pharmaceuticals and food-processing industries. Its development illustrates the importance of transport facilities, electricity, urban markets, industrial infrastructure and access to ports.

Public-sector industrialisation helped create new industrial centres, but a balanced industrial economy required more than establishing factories. Roads, electricity, water, skills, finance and market access were also necessary.

Prelims focus

  • Industrial Policy Resolution: 1948 and 1956.
  • IPR 1956: Schedule A contained 17 industries; Schedule B contained 12 industries.
  • Industries (Development and Regulation) Act: 1951; Sections 11 and 13 dealt with licensing and related controls.
  • Bhilai: Soviet Union; Rourkela: West Germany; Durgapur: United Kingdom.
  • SAIL was incorporated in 1973.
  • Gujarat Industrial Region: its nucleus lies between Ahmedabad and Vadodara.
  • Trap: The 1956 Resolution did not eliminate private enterprise; it strengthened public-sector leadership within a mixed economy.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class XI Economics, Chapter 2, Indian Economy 1950–1990, pp. 17–31; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class XII Geography, Chapter 8, Manufacturing Industries, pp. 85–103; Government of India, Industrial Policy Resolution, 30 April 1956, paragraphs 5, 15 and 18 and Schedules A and B; India Code, Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, Sections 11 and 13; Yojana, May 1965, The Steel Industry and the Three Public Sector Steel Plants, p. 394; Steel Authority of India Limited, Background and History; Ministry of Steel, Modernisation of Steel Plants, 25 July 2022. Online sources consulted on 22 November 2026.]

body:
Changing agricultural relations after independence

Agriculture was the main source of livelihood for a large proportion of India's population at independence. However, land ownership was unequal, agricultural productivity was low and many cultivators worked as tenants under landlords or intermediaries.

Independent India therefore pursued land reforms to change agricultural ownership and tenancy relations. The purpose was to reduce exploitation, improve the position of cultivators and create conditions for higher agricultural productivity.

Major land reform measures

MeasureMeaning and objective
Abolition of intermediariesRemoval of zamindars and other revenue-collecting intermediaries between the State and cultivators.
Tenancy reformsRegulation of rents, security of tenure and, where permitted, transfer of ownership rights to cultivating tenants.
Land ceilingFixing a maximum limit on individual or family landholdings and redistributing surplus land.
Consolidation of holdingsCombining fragmented agricultural plots into more compact holdings.

Abolition of zamindari was relatively more successful than other land reform measures. Tenancy reforms and land ceiling laws faced difficulties because of weak implementation, legal exemptions, incomplete land records and evasion of the rules. Consequently, unequal land distribution and landlessness continued in many areas.

Land reforms and Green Revolution are different

Land reforms change the ownership and tenancy structure of agriculture. The Green Revolution changes agricultural production through improved seeds, irrigation, fertilizers, pesticides and machinery. Higher productivity does not automatically produce equal land ownership.

The Green Revolution in India

The Green Revolution refers to the substantial increase in agricultural productivity achieved through the introduction of high-yielding varieties of seeds and a package of modern agricultural inputs and practices.

India faced serious food shortages during the mid-1960s. Droughts and inadequate domestic food production increased dependence on imported foodgrains. The government therefore introduced a new agricultural strategy to increase domestic food production and reduce dependence on imports.

The introduction of the new agricultural strategy

The High Yielding Varieties Programme (HYVP) was introduced on a wider scale during 1966–1967. It initially concentrated on selected agricultural regions and particularly emphasised wheat production.

Important developments included:

  • Norman Borlaug: Developed high-yielding Mexican semi-dwarf wheat varieties that became important to the international Green Revolution.
  • M.S. Swaminathan: Played a leading scientific role in adapting and promoting improved wheat varieties under Indian conditions. He is widely known as the Father of India's Green Revolution.
  • C. Subramaniam: Provided important political and administrative leadership for the introduction of the new agricultural strategy as Union Agriculture Minister during the period.
  • ICAR and IARI: Indian agricultural research institutions contributed to testing, adapting, multiplying and distributing improved varieties.

In 1966–1967, India imported approximately 18,000 tonnes of Mexican wheat seed as part of the large-scale introduction of high-yielding wheat varieties.

The expression Green Revolution was coined by William S. Gaud in 1968. The Indian agricultural programme had already begun through the introduction of the new technology in 1966–1967.

The technology package

The Green Revolution was not simply the distribution of improved seeds. High-yielding varieties required reliable irrigation, adequate nutrients and protection from pests. Their full productivity could be achieved only when several complementary inputs were available together.

  • High-yielding variety seeds: Improved wheat and rice varieties with higher yield potential under suitable conditions.
  • Irrigation: Assured water supply through canals, wells and tube wells, reducing dependence on uncertain rainfall.
  • Chemical fertilizers: Supply of essential plant nutrients to support higher crop yields.
  • Pesticides and herbicides: Control of insects, diseases and weeds that could damage crops.
  • Farm machinery: Tractors, pump sets, threshers and other equipment to improve farm operations.
  • Institutional support: Agricultural credit, extension services, assured prices and government procurement arrangements.

Why the package mattered

HYV seeds alone could not guarantee high yields. Without adequate water and nutrients, improved varieties could fail to achieve their yield potential. Irrigation, fertilizers, pest control, credit and other supporting facilities were essential.

Regional spread of the Green Revolution

The initial benefits were concentrated in relatively prosperous and well-irrigated agricultural regions. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh became important centres of the new wheat-growing strategy. Parts of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu also adopted improved agricultural practices during the early phase.

The first phase is generally associated with the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. During the second phase, from the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s, the technology spread to additional regions and crops. However, rain-fed and less-developed agricultural regions did not benefit equally.

Important agricultural concepts

Multiple cropping

Multiple cropping means growing more than one crop on the same agricultural land during a year. For example, a farmer may grow a wheat crop during winter and another crop during the following season. Reliable irrigation and suitable crop varieties make multiple cropping possible.

Modern farming method

The modern farming method refers to the use of improved seeds together with fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation and machinery. It is a broader technological package, not simply the practice of growing multiple crops.

Marketed surplus

Marketed surplus is the portion of agricultural production that a farmer actually sells in the market. An increase in agricultural output can increase the quantity of marketed surplus available for procurement and trade.

Prelims focus

  • India's High Yielding Varieties Programme began on a wider scale in 1966–1967.
  • Approximately 18,000 tonnes of Mexican wheat seed were imported in 1966–1967.
  • Norman Borlaug developed important Mexican semi-dwarf wheat varieties; M.S. Swaminathan was a leading Indian scientific contributor.
  • C. Subramaniam provided important political leadership for the new agricultural strategy.
  • Early adoption was concentrated in irrigated regions, including the Punjab-Haryana-western Uttar Pradesh wheat belt.
  • Trap: Multiple cropping and modern farming methods are related but are not the same concept.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class XI Economics, Chapter 2, Indian Economy 1950–1990, pp. 17–31; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class XII Geography, Chapter 5, Land Resources and Agriculture, pp. 40–59; NCERT, Economics, Class IX, Chapter 1, The Story of Village Palampur, pp. 1–15; Indian Council of Agricultural Research, M.S. Swaminathan's historical account of the Green Revolution and the 1966–1967 High Yielding Varieties Programme; Norman Borlaug, Nobel Lecture, 11 December 1970; William S. Gaud, The Green Revolution: Accomplishments and Apprehensions, 8 March 1968. Online sources consulted on 22 November 2026.]
